Separately, the construction argument was never sound: after cutting MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM my long book is healthcare, consumer finance, payments, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, energy and biotech, with genuine Nasdaq loading of roughly QCOM 6.5% plus PYPL 7.5% - about 14% of NAV. Hedging that with 21% of QQQ is a deliberate net short of a factor I no longer own, which adds residual variance instead of removing it, and it is the leg that bleeds if the AI complex keeps squeezing. So I move to 24% SPY / 13% QQQ: total short-side beta goes from about 40.2 to about 38.9 (net index beta still roughly flat, still a spread bet and not a market bet), gross stays 98%, cash stays 2%, and the hedge's tech loading now matches the tech the basket actually holds. Only two legs trade - roughly 16% of NAV of notional at ~2bps a side, on the order of 0.3bp of NAV - a trivial price for deleting an unmandated factor bet, and I am paying it on nothing else. Everything about the long basket, its stops and its take-profits stands exactly as filled.

decisions.name: Opus 5 pairs

decisions.reason: Nothing has changed that my 07-30 analysis did not already price, and the one piece of genuinely new information cuts in favour of the book rather than against it: MA's beat and Visa's severance-inflated opex confirm the direction of the pair I trimmed, so if anything I was too conservative there, not wrong. A pairs book earns its return from spreads reverting over weeks, not from being re-optimised every session; the 250-day z-scores that selected these five pairs cannot have moved materially in one trading day, and the half-lives I underwrote (34 days on TSM/KLAC, 46 on the pairs I kept) are measured in weeks. Rebalancing now would pay ~2bps a side a second time on legs whose entry costs I settled yesterday, to chase a fractional resize justified by one day of price action — that is churn, a guaranteed cost against an unquantified benefit. The specific temptation is to upsize MA/V on the earnings evidence, and I am declining it for the same reason I trimmed it on 07-30: MA/V carries only ~4% spread vol, so even a full 1sd convergence is worth little per dollar of gross, and confirming the fundamental story does not raise the pair's productivity per unit of scarce capital. The adverse datapoint — momentum's 5%+ month-end rally — is not a reason to cut MTUM either, because it occurred before my fill, so I am short the crowded factor at a higher price than my thesis assumed and my expected reversion is larger, not smaller. The China-DUV catalyst behind the semi rout is also more damaging to semicap tooling than to the foundry, which supports the TSM-long/KLAC-short orientation I already hold. I am leaving stop-losses and take-profits off deliberately: on a beta-matched spread book a stop converts a hedged pair into a naked directional leg exactly when the spread is widest and expected return is highest, systematically monetising my worst entries. Aggregate net SPY beta stays near flat after the XLU/D exit, and cash stays at zero because 4% APY on idle cash is worth about 1bp a week against the convergence I am underwriting. Every position's thesis stands unamended.

decisions.reason: Not one market session has elapsed since this book filled — the 07-30 orders printed at the 07-31 close, so I am being asked to re-trade a portfolio whose ink is still wet, and every leg I changed would pay entry costs a second time. More importantly, the evidence that arrived since I decided argues the same way I did rather than against me. The IEF short, my biggest change (4 -> 17), got the 10y closing at 4.75% and the 30y at 5.23%, a 19-year high, with September hike odds at 53-60% against an economist consensus of no hike; that leg is early, not late. The QQQ cut (20 -> 6) got a July in which the Nasdaq fell ~9.7% from June while the Dow made a fourth straight monthly gain — the exact growth-to-cyclical rotation the XLI/XLF/KRE overweights are built to harvest — and because my fill was at the 07-31 close I sold the stub into a +1% Nasdaq day rather than into a flush. GLD is already through $4,100 against the $4,066 I sized at. The one genuinely new fact that cuts against me is the pause in US strikes on Iran with a Hormuz compromise being negotiated, which threatens the war premium under the gold and oil-inflation legs — but Brent held $88-92 straight through that headline and gold rose anyway, so the de-escalation is not yet doing the damage it could, and GLD is deliberately my hedge rather than a directional war bet. Both are reasons not to add to those legs, which is what holding does; neither is a reason to pay costs to cut a position I set at deliberately moderate size two days ago. Finally, my mandate has pre-committed rotation dates — Oct-1 and Nov-1 — and the 6% cash exists to fund the XLP re-entry then. Today is neither of those dates. Trading here would be churn dressed as diligence.

The corroboration is dead too: the move came from Amazon +15.3% on AWS growth of 37%, and with Amazon plus Tesla at ~40% of the fund, XLY is an AI-capex proxy, not the discretionary-wallet squeeze I underwrote. New leg, funded out of ERX, and the point of it is that it carries the same driver as MPC with the binary event already behind it. That means it partially survives the one scenario that kills the rest of this book: on a durable ceasefire, crude collapses and ERX halves the move twice over, but refiners get cheaper feedstock against sticky product prices and cracks can widen before they narrow. The funding short, rebuilt correctly. decisions.name: Opus 5 vol regime
decisions.research_notes: Checked the 2026-07-31 session, which is the only new information since my 7/30 decision (that decision was made on 7/29 data and filled at the 7/31 close). Findings: (1) VOL REGIME RESET — VIX went 20.66 (7/29) to ~17.09 (7/30) to ~16.0-16.4 (7/31), a ~22% collapse, as the AAPL/AMZN catalyst chain resolved benignly; SPY +0.7%, Nasdaq +1%, Dow +0.5% on AI-capex strength (AMZN surged). Against SPY 20d realized of roughly 13-14%, the variance risk premium is now ~2-3 points, not the ~7 points my SVXY leg was explicitly sized to harvest. My book filled AT that close, so the collapse is in my entry marks, not my P&L. (2) MACRO TAIL WIDENED — 10y Treasury closed 4.75%, highest since January 2025, driven by $100 oil on an escalating Middle East conflict plus Fed speakers reinforcing the case for higher rates. This is a correlation-raising shock and the main forward threat to the dispersion half of my regime call. (3) STRESS-TESTED MY OWN CORE — iShares' fund page confirms USMV is 31.82% Information Technology and 6.96% utilities, versus SPLV at ~1.78% tech and ~25.4% utilities, because USMV normalizes to MSCI USA sector weights while SPLV is an unconstrained 100-lowest-vol screen. This looked like a construction error arguing to flip my weights, and SPLV's YTD +9.5% vs USMV's +4.63% supported that. It does not hold: MSCI's min-vol optimizer screens out high-vol names, so USMV's tech sleeve is low-beta software/services, not semis — confirmed directly by USMV falling 0.21% on 7/29 while SMH fell 4.79% and SPY fell 1.54%. USMV stays the larger leg. (4) Checked SPLV's rate exposure since 25% utilities into a 19-month-high 10y is the obvious objection — the headwind is not biting, SPLV is +3.92% over the past month and within ~1% of its 52-week high through the entire rate move. Issuer data: USMV 3yr beta 0.49, expense 0.15%; SPLV yield ~2.2%.

decisions.reason: I am not touching the equity core, which is a session old and needs no change; I am closing the two carry legs because one had its premise refuted overnight and the other was already refuted by my own arithmetic. SVXY existed to harvest the gap between implied and realized index vol. When I sized it that gap was ~7 points; after VIX collapsed 22% to ~16 against SPY realized of ~13-14% it is ~2-3 points. Getting paid 2-3 points to be short the tail is thin at the best of times, and this is not the best of times: the 10y just broke to 4.75% on $100 oil and an escalating Middle East conflict, which is precisely the macro shock that drags implied correlation back up and hurts a short-index-vol position most. The carry shrank and the tail fattened simultaneously, so the leg goes. The TQQQ/SQQQ pair is me correcting a documented mistake rather than reacting to news: on 7/30 I wrote that my own backtest gives it ~1.2%/yr on notional against 3% APR borrow on EACH leg — roughly -0.25% of NAV per year with a -27.76% worst 63-day — and then kept it at 7+7 anyway because it 'expressed the regime.' That was attachment to a narrative over my own numbers. It is a negative-carry structure whose best environment is chop and whose worst is trend, and an oil-and-rates shock is a trending catalyst, so the case only got weaker. Closing both costs about 26% turnover at ~2-2.5bps, roughly $0.07, and it is economically positive from day one: I stop paying 0.42%/yr of NAV in borrow and start earning 4% on the cash. VIXY goes up rather than down as the exact mirror of my 7/30 trim — I cut it then because buying insurance at VIX 20.66 right after a pop is paying up post-event, and the same insurance now costs ~22% less in VIX terms while the event it insures against became materially more likely. Buy convexity when it is cheap and the tail is fat; that is the discipline, and it is the reason I can still run an 78% low-vol equity core. The 16% cash is deliberate, not a residual: with my short-vol carry removed and a live geopolitical/inflation catalyst, dry powder that pays 4% is the right way to hold risk in reserve, and it funds adding to the core if the rate shock hands me a better entry. Net result is a simpler book, lower gross, no borrow, more cash yield, and my two best-evidenced legs plus a cheap hedge.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to constrain; regardless, this book is now differentiated by holding zero short legs and zero leveraged-ETF structures, expressing the vol view solely through a long-only min-vol core plus a single long-convexity VIXY sleeve funded by a 16% cash reserve — the opposite construction from the short-gamma, short-variance carry stack it replaces.

positions.thesis: I attacked this leg with the strongest objection available and it survived, which is why it grows rather than shrinks. The objection: iShares' own page shows USMV at 31.82% Information Technology, seemingly absurd in a book whose central claim is that the tech/semi complex is the source of the tape's volatility, and SPLV's YTD +9.5% against USMV's +4.63% says the market agrees. The rebuttal is that the sector label conflates two unlike things — MSCI's minimum-volatility optimizer explicitly excludes high-volatility constituents, so USMV's tech weight sits in low-beta software, services and payments, not semiconductors. That is not theory: on 29-Jul USMV fell 0.21% while SMH fell 4.79% and SPY fell 1.54%. No fund with genuine semi exposure posts a 14% downside capture on a day the semis drop nearly 5%. So USMV's low measured vol is real rather than an artifact, and it is also the leg with the lowest rate sensitivity in my core at just 6.96% utilities, which matters now that the 10y is at 4.75%. 20d realized vol 9.97% against SPY 11.65%; 3yr beta 0.49 per the issuer; expense 0.15%. Upsized from 44% because closing two negative-carry legs freed budget and this is the position I have the most direct evidence for. The -14% stop is a regime-break brake rather than a trading stop, capping this leg near -6.4% of NAV.

Held for the concentration USMV structurally cannot provide: 1.78% technology versus USMV's 31.82%, because SPLV is an unconstrained screen of the 100 lowest-volatility S&P 500 names while USMV must normalize to its parent index's sector weights. That makes SPLV the only sleeve in the book with essentially zero semiconductor exposure at the moment my regime call identifies semis as the vol source, which is why it belongs alongside USMV rather than instead of it — the two funds fail in different states, and owning both is the actual diversification. The live objection is rates: ~25.4% utilities into a 10y at 4.75%, its highest since January 2025, on an oil-driven inflation impulse. I checked whether that is biting and it is not — SPLV is +9.5% YTD and +3.92% over the past month, trading within about 1% of its 52-week high straight through the rate move, so the market is treating these as defensives rather than bond proxies. The ~2.2% yield also pays me to wait, roughly a point better than USMV. Kept smaller than USMV because its 20d realized vol of 14.88% is half again USMV's and my vol-target rule tilts the core toward the lower-vol construction. The stop stays wider at -16% precisely so ordinary rate noise in the utility sleeve cannot stop me out of a position I hold for its tech-free composition.

Sized up from 4% as the exact inverse of the reasoning that made me trim it a session ago. On 30-Jul I cut this leg because adding vol insurance at VIX 20.66 immediately after a 13.5% spike is paying up for a hedge post-event. VIX has since collapsed to roughly 16, so the identical protection is about 22% cheaper in VIX terms — while the risk it protects against grew materially, with $100 oil, an escalating Middle East conflict, the 10y at a 19-month high of 4.75% and Fed speakers reinforcing higher-for-longer. Selling insurance when it is expensive and buying it when it is cheap is the entire discipline; doing the reverse is how vol books die. This is now the book's only long-volatility expression, replacing the short TQQQ/SQQQ pair, and it is a strictly better one: it is genuinely convex and costs a known contango bleed rather than an unknown trend tax with a -27.76% tail. That bleed is real at roughly 43.8%/yr, about 0.22% of NAV per month at this weight, and it is the price of letting me carry a 78% equity core into a fattening macro tail. The +50% take-profit is unchanged and still correctly calibrated after the reset: off the lower futures basis it corresponds to VIX in the high-20s to 30, a genuine dislocation worth converting into cash rather than round-tripping. No stop, because stopping out of insurance at the moment it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never do.

decisions.name: Opus Momentum

(4) Apple beat ($2.02 vs $1.89, rev $109.4bn, iPhone +22%) but fell 7.3% on a soft September guide, a services miss and Cook flagging a chip-supply squeeze raising costs - so AAPL's trend broke and its "anti-capex" virtue became the wrong side of the trade. decisions.reason: My short sleeve was built on one explicit claim, which I wrote down: hyperscalers are trapped, because cutting capex collapses orders and keeping capex gets the stock hit like Meta's was. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.

HBM is sold out through 2026 under multi-year agreements, DRAM rose 90% in Q1 with suppliers guiding a further 10-20% per month into year-end, and Micron forecasts shortage beyond 2026. +212% YTD and +637% over a year makes it the strongest trend in my mandate's named universe; largest weight, wide -18% stop because its realised volatility is extreme and a tight stop would just donate the position to noise.

A genuinely distinct driver from memory pricing and from broad semis beta, so it diversifies the sleeve instead of levering it.

My mandate's named leveraged instrument, now pointed the right way: 3x semis beta from only 5% of capital. decisions.name: Opus Value

decisions.reason: I got the SOXL short wrong and new evidence arrived within one session. Worse, SOXL is now 69.5% below its 52-week high after a 65.5% collapse in July, so calling it a still-frothy 3x fund was stale framing; I was momentum-shorting an asset that has already crashed, which is precisely the behaviour my mandate was written after backtests to forbid, and a 3x instrument down 70% carries violent upside convexity against a short. I exit the short entirely rather than trim, because there is no version of my contrarian mean-reversion mandate in which the most oversold thing in my universe is a short. I do not flip it long: the rebound reads as short-covering rather than fresh demand and the Chinese state-backed capacity story is unchanged, so no conviction means no position. The freed notional goes to the depressed quality longs the mandate actually exists to own, plus a new ServiceNow starter as the deepest dislocation available, plus gold, which broke $4,100 while 30-year yields hit their highest since 2007 — strength against its worst macro headwind, and now my only hedge. XLV is cut because July sector data showed healthcare as the worst-performing sector at -0.78%, so the thematic wrapper is unconfirmed even though the UNH-specific fundamentals are. Crypto is untouched because nothing changed and spot costs 35bps a side.

Down 34% year to date at 2.96x forward sales, cheaper than Adobe on the identical measure, and it jumped 7% to $176 in the late-July enterprise-software reversal alongside ServiceNow +8% and Workday +10%. The 'AI kills software' discount is visibly closing and this is the cheapest large-cap way to own that closing.

Gold broke above $4,100 after five weeks of consolidation and did so while the 30-year Treasury yield reached its highest level since 2007 at 5.25% — that is strength shown against its single worst macro headwind, which is a better signal than a rally on falling rates would be. With the SOXL short removed this is now the book's only hedge, and Iranian attacks on escorted tankers in the Strait of Hormuz are precisely the tail it is here to cover.

Raised 11->12. Down 32.9% year to date, roughly 15x earnings with revenue +11.5% and earnings +28%, and it rallied 7% to $241 in the same software reversal. A high-retention subscription business priced for terminal decline is the purest available expression of this mandate. Sized as a starter rather than a core because 30-year yields at their highest since 2007 are a genuine headwind to long-duration multiples and I would rather average in than anchor on one bounce.

Held flat at 6%. Near $63,900 it is still roughly half off its high, which keeps a residual oversold long consistent with the mandate, but the Fed held rates and ETF flows remain poor so there is still no near-term catalyst to justify more. Paying 35bps to adjust a position on no news would be pure cost.

decisions.reason: One leg broke and one new leader was confirmed; everything else is untouched because nothing in it changed. Apple's binary event resolved against the position exactly as I framed it: revenue and EPS beat, but Services missed by roughly $500m, Greater China came in light, and September-quarter guidance of +9-11% undershot the +12% modeled, with Barclays and others calling services deceleration and China structural rather than transitory. The stock fell 7.2%. A trend follower does not hold a leader that has just broken down on guidance — the whole point of the tight stop and reduced size was to make this exit cheap, and taking it is the discipline, not a reversal. Amazon is the replacement the tape handed me on the same day: up about 15%, its biggest single-day move since 2012, on AWS accelerating to +36.7% with a $496bn backlog, revenue +20% and operating income +43%. That is demonstrated relative strength with quality confirmation, and critically it sits on the monetization side of AI rather than the hardware side that is still cracking, so it does not rebuild the semiconductor concentration I spent last week removing. XLE stays the anchor because its trend was confirmed hard this week — crude up more than 20% in July on Hormuz tanker attacks and falling inventories. I deliberately do not press XLE further despite that: a geopolitical risk premium reverses violently on a single diplomatic headline, and the US has already paused airstrikes once. I also do not add back the semiconductor sleeve despite SOXX +8% and Micron +18%, because the analysis of that move reads as short covering rather than fresh demand and a trend follower needs a confirmed signal, not a bounce.

Held at 12%. Rising long yields are a mild headwind to dividend carry, but this sleeve exists to dampen drawdown while leadership reforms, and this week proves leadership is still reforming — a single session produced Amazon +15%, Apple -7.2% and an 8% semiconductor bounce. Getting paid to wait through that dispersion is the point, and trimming it to chase the same week's winner would be exactly backwards.

Held at 12%. With the 10-year above 4.7% and the 30-year at its highest level since 2007, high return-on-equity businesses with low leverage are the part of the equity complex least damaged by a repricing of the cost of capital, because they do not need the capital. It keeps me inside the factor mandate without rebuilding the high-beta exposure that broke it.

Held at 10%. Realized volatility in the mega-cap complex is elevated — Apple down 7.2% and Amazon up 15% in the same session — and written-call premium is richest exactly when that is true, so this sleeve's carry improves precisely as my directional sleeves get noisier. It remains the most counter-cyclical income available inside the mandate.

Held at 10%. A 65% one-month collapse in a 3x semiconductor fund followed by an 8% single-day index bounce, alongside double-digit single-session moves in two of the largest companies in the world, is a volatility-regime signal rather than noise. Low-volatility equity is the trend-compatible way to stay fully engaged through a regime like that instead of retreating to cash.

New 8% position funded by the Apple exit and two points of cash. Q2 net sales rose 20% to $200.6bn with operating income up 43% and AWS growth accelerating to +36.7% on a $496bn backlog, and the stock rose about 15% — its largest single-day gain in over a decade — with Wells Fargo, Citi and Wedbush reiterating buys. That is a demonstrated relative-strength leader with quality confirmation rather than a valuation guess, and it expresses AI through cloud monetization rather than the hardware cycle that is still unstable. The 12% stop is deliberately tight because I am entering immediately after a gap and gaps can retrace.

Held at 6%. Semis bounced hard this week with SOXX +8% and Micron +18%, but that move is characterized as short covering and bargain hunting rather than fresh demand, so I neither add back the weight I cut nor cut further on a signal I do not trust in either direction. The residual exists so the index's own reconstitution mechanically rotates me out of fading names and into the next leaders without my having to forecast them.

decisions.reason: I got the biggest thing wrong and the cost of admitting it one session in is about 0.2bp, so I am admitting it. My 18% SMH short was explicitly justified by a live catalyst - hyperscaler capex doubt plus SK Hynix's guidance miss - and that catalyst did not fade, it inverted: Microsoft's AI business grew 123% with Azure accelerating, Amazon's cloud beat, Big Tech capex is tracking ~$650bn for 2026, and SK Hynix and Samsung printed their best days on record. That is a demand confirmation for the exact cohort I am short, not sentiment noise, and the split reaction - Meta -8% for refusing a capex outlook on the same day MSFT had its best session since 2008 - shows a market discriminating between AI spenders and AI beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale, with semis on the receiving end of the spend. What survives is only the weak half of my case, 'it went up 80% so it must fall', which is not an edge and has bankrupted better shorts than me. So the hedge goes back to the mandate's own word - SMALL - at 6%, exactly where it stood before I tripled it. I am not flipping to long semis and I am not switching vehicles: I checked ARKK and it is flat over twelve months, so it is not stretched and would be a worse short. I add 3 points to CVX because genuinely new information landed after my fill - Chevron reported adjusted $6.06 against $5.11 consensus, a 19% beat, with production up 20%, record US output, Hess synergies and a fresh dividend, none of which is in my mark, against Brent up over 20% on the month with tankers being hit in Hormuz. PFE, VZ, VLO and MO are untouched - nothing about their theses changed in two sessions, and PFE's 8/4 print is a reason to sit still rather than trade.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to breach; what distinguishes this book is that it is long the cash-generative, non-duration value cohort - pharma near its 52-week low, a bank at 11x, integrated oil and refining into a Hormuz supply shock, and telecom - while carrying only a token short in the cohort that has just demonstrated its earnings, rather than a large directional bet against AI.
